title: What goes into our post-tour follow-up

content.job: Standalone list email. Tell the full exchange from more tours and unanswered follow-up to the client's within-a-week practice and prospective texts. Connect the point to the complete LeadLock system with one reply invitation.
content.body:
She told me she pays attention to whether her venue is the first stop on a couple's tour list or the last one.

When she knows it's the last, she reaches out within a week. She asks them, politely but directly, whether they've picked their venue or are still deciding. It's a question that fits a couple who has finished looking.

A couple fresh off their first tour is in a different place. They're still comparing, and they may not be ready to answer that.

**Knowing a couple toured your venue isn't the same as knowing they're ready to decide.**

She already had automated follow-up emails in place, and she was reaching out personally on top of them. She raised the idea of adding texts after the tour, and I agreed we could incorporate them.

That conversation is a good picture of how we think about follow-up. You're already generating inquiries, hosting tours and talking with couples yourself. The support around that work should build on what you learn during the visit, so a couple who's still comparing and a couple who's ready to decide each hear something that fits where they are.

LeadLock is the platform where we build your email and text follow-up. Inside it, we set up The Foolproof Follow-Up Advantage, the email-and-text system that carries your own conversations forward between visits. You run the platform, and the personal contact couples get from you stays yours.
content.ending:
If you'd like follow-up support shaped around what you learn on your tours, simply reply to this email and let's talk about your business.

Talk soon,
Whitney

content.title: First tour or last tour
content.script:
I had a call with one of our venue clients recently, and she was booking more tours, but more of those couples were going quiet afterwards.

So I asked her a question. When couples leave a tour, do they still have other venues to see, or are they ready to move forward?

And she explained that she gauges one thing: is her venue their first tour, or their last?

When she knows it's their last, she reaches out within a week and asks, really politely, if they've made their choice or they're still undecided.

I thought that was such a smart distinction.

Because a couple who's just started touring is still comparing, right? They're not necessarily ready for that question yet.

Now, she already had automated emails going out, and she was following up personally on top of that. She'd been thinking about texting couples after the tour, too, and I told her we could add that.

So when we shape follow-up after a tour, the fact that a couple visited is only part of the picture. We want to know what they're ready to do next, so every email and text supports the conversation you're already having with them.

caption.body:
One still has other venues on the list. The other may have just finished looking. From your inbox, the days after can look exactly alike, and it's hard to know which message each of them needs.

I asked one of our venue clients about this on a recent call: when couples leave, are they still exploring or close to deciding? She told me she pays close attention to where her venue lands in their search.

If she knows it's the final visit, she gets in touch within a week and asks, kindly and plainly, whether they've decided or are still weighing options. A couple at the start of their search may not be ready for that.

She already sent automated emails and reached out to couples herself, and she brought up adding texts after tours. I told her we could incorporate them.

That's the information we want shaping follow-up: what the couple was ready to do when the tour ended, more than the fact that a tour happened. Then each message fits the stage they've reached, and your own conversations with couples stay at the center.
caption.hook: Two couples can walk out of the same venue tour at very different points in their search.

beats: Open on the tension: Google Ads leads dipped in August while tours stayed steady.
The client asks what WIA is seeing for leads from Facebook versus Google.
Meta brought far more August leads; Google dipped and WIA is digging into it.
Whitney explains, hedged, that Google ads or organic search may work together with Meta retargeting.

content.title: Reading a Google dip against steady tours
content.script:
One of our venue clients saw her Google Ads leads dip from July to August. Over those same months, her tour numbers stayed about the same. So which number tells you more?

She asked me on a recent call what we were seeing for leads from Facebook versus Google. And on lead count alone, Meta brought in way more in August. Meta held steady, Google took a dip, and we're digging into that.

But the lead count is only one piece. Somebody might see her Google ad, or find her through organic search, and then get retargeted with a Meta ad. Those could all be working together, right?

And when I looked past the leads, her tour volume had stayed pretty steady month over month. So in theory, more of those leads were turning into tours. It also looked like bookings were up from July to August.

That's why I don't want to judge a channel by its lead count by itself. So before deciding what her dip meant, I looked at what happened after her inquiries came in: the tours, the bookings, and how the two channels might be working together.

So we're still looking into the Google side, just with her tours and bookings in front of us too.

caption.body:
You open the report, see fewer leads from Google than the month before, and start wondering whether the budget is in the right place.

A venue client asked us something similar recently: which channel was bringing in more leads, Facebook or Google? In August, Meta had brought in far more, and Google's count had slipped from July. We're looking into why.

Her tours, though, held steady month over month, and it looked like bookings were up as well. Her two channels might not have been working separately, either. One might find her on Google, from an ad or an ordinary search, and later come across a Meta ad. Both could be part of the same decision.

So before drawing conclusions about her Google numbers, we looked at what happened once couples inquired: how many came out to tour, how many booked, and how the platforms might be supporting each other. A dip is a reason to look closer, with the tour calendar as part of what we read.

content.job: Lets a cold viewer see, from a venue client's own five-year read, that couples almost always decide after the visit rather than on it.
beats: Use ordinary, non-client-specific workday b-roll; do not suggest footage of the actual call or venue.

content.title: Couples decide after the tour

caption.body:
If you've hosted a lot of tours, you probably have a feel for this already. One of our venue clients put it plainly: in five years, only a handful of couples have booked on the spot.

She described two kinds of couples who come through. Some already know the venue, love it and have been waiting for it, but still want to see a few other places before they commit. In her experience, those are the couples her venue books most often. Others are earlier in the process, touring several venues while they work out what they want.

Either way, the decision usually lands in the days after the visit. That's why what she picks up during a tour is worth carrying into what couples hear from her next.

When we shape post-tour emails and texts with a venue, that's the knowledge we want built in: who the couple seemed to be as they walked through, and what they're likely ready for now.

before_publishing.text:
A line a person wrote for the earlier Reel 3 was not carried into its new premise: More tours are a good sign. But a tour on your calendar doesn't tell you whether the couple is on their first visit or their last, and unanswered follow-up looks the same either way.

This came up with one of our venue clients. I asked whether couples left planning other visits or ready to move forward. Her answer was that she watches whether her venue opened their search or closed it.

When she knows they've finished touring, she reaches out within a week and politely asks if they've landed on a venue or are still undecided. A couple who has only begun visiting is still comparing what they've seen.

She already paired automated emails with her personal contact, and she asked about texting couples after the tour as well. I said we could add that.

That's the kind of detail we want shaping the emails and texts around your conversations, so each couple hears from you in a way that suits how far their search has come.
